notes.meaning: John writes like a loving, aged father to his "little children." His goal is that they not sin at all. But if a believer does sin, he should not give up hope. Jesus stands before the Father like a defense lawyer who pleads for us, and he can do this because he is righteous and has no sin of his own.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching sees Christ as the one Savior whose sacrifice pleads for us. It also asks the saints in heaven to pray for believers, and it treats that as a different kind of help from Christ's.

notes.meaning: An "atoning sacrifice" is an offering that takes away sin and turns away God's just anger. Jesus himself is that sacrifice, and what he pleads before the Father is his own death for us. Its reach is not limited to John's first readers. It extends to "the whole world."

differ.view: "The whole world" means believers of every nation, place and age, not every single person. Christ's sacrifice is for all who will believe, wherever they are.
Christ's sacrifice reaches as far as sin reaches, to all people. Limiting it to some is wrong.
You are part of "the whole world," so you may be sure Christ died for you too, not only for great saints like Peter and Paul.

notes.meaning: How can we be sure we really know God? We can tell by whether we keep his commands. This does not mean flawless obedience. It means a heart that gladly accepts God's will. Obedience does not earn our place with God, but it is the evidence that our faith is real.

Some people say "I know God" but ignore what he commands, and their claim is false. True knowledge of God always changes how a person lives. John is likely answering teachers who boasted of special knowledge while living careless lives.

When someone keeps God's word, their love for God has grown full and mature. This is not a claim to be sinless. It means love and obedience belong together, so each shows the other is real. That gives us assurance that we are truly joined to God.
To "abide" means to stay or remain joined to Christ. Anyone who claims this should live the way Jesus lived. That means his everyday life of love and obedience to the Father, not his miracles.

The command John means, to love, is not new teaching. The readers had heard it from the moment they first heard the gospel. Unlike the false teachers with their novel ideas, John simply repeats what they already know.

Yet it is also a new command, because Jesus himself called it new and gave it a new reason: love one another as he loved us. It was shown first in Jesus, and now it shows in his followers. The darkness of sin and ignorance is passing away like night at dawn, and the true light of Christ is already shining.

Some people claim to live in God's light while hating a fellow believer, and they are still in the dark. "Brother" here mainly means a fellow Christian. Love for each other is a key test of whether faith is real.

Whoever loves fellow believers stays in the light. There is nothing in him to make him trip, and he will not be a stumbling block that leads others into sin. Love guards both his own steps and his brother's.

Hatred, even a simple lack of love, keeps a person in darkness. Like someone walking at night, he cannot see where his life is heading, because the darkness has blinded him. John learned this himself: as a young man he once wanted to call fire down on people who rejected Jesus.

"Little children" here most likely means all believers, spoken to with fatherly love. Every believer, even the newest, is fully forgiven. That forgiveness comes "through His name," because of who Jesus is and what he did, not because of our own merit. It is the foundation everything else is built on.

John speaks to three groups, which many read as stages of Christian growth. "Fathers" are mature believers who know Christ, who has existed from the beginning. "Young men" are in the thick of the fight and have beaten the devil, and their strength comes from God's word living in them. "Children" know God as their Father. The repetition adds emphasis, and "I have written" refers to this same letter.

"The world" here does not mean the planet or its people, whom God loves. It means human life and values set against God. Believers must not give their hearts to it, because the heart cannot hold love for the world and love for the Father at the same time.

John names three things the world offers. The first is the desires of the flesh, meaning craving bodily pleasure. The second is the desires of the eyes, meaning craving riches and showy things. The third is the pride of life, meaning showing off and chasing praise. None of these comes from the Father. Enjoying good things is not wrong; the problem comes when they become what we live for.
The world and everything people crave in it is already fading away. Whoever does God's will has built on something that cannot pass away, and that person will last forever.

"The last hour" is the final age before Christ returns, and we still live in it. An "antichrist" is someone who opposes Christ. Believers had been taught that one great enemy of Christ would come. Many smaller antichrists, false teachers, had already appeared, which showed that the last age had begun.
These false teachers had once been part of the church, but they left. John says they never truly belonged in their hearts, or they would have stayed. Their leaving made plain what they really were.

differ.view: This verse shows that true believers will keep going to the end. Those who fall away prove they were never truly saved.
Their hearts had already left God before they left the church. "Not of us" also means they were never sent by the apostles to teach.

notes.meaning: The "anointing" is the Holy Spirit, given by Christ, the Holy One. It is like the oil once poured on priests and kings. Because of the Spirit, believers know all they need for faith and for spotting error. It does not mean they know everything.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The best ancient copies read "you all know" rather than "you know all things." On that reading, the point is that the Spirit is given to every Christian, not to a select few.

notes.meaning: John is not writing because they are ignorant. He writes because they already know the truth. Knowing the truth helps you spot a lie, just as a straight line shows up a crooked one.

The great lie is denying that Jesus is the Christ, the promised Savior. Some teachers in John's day split the man Jesus from "the Christ." Whoever denies the Son in this way also denies the Father, and that is the spirit of antichrist.
No one can have the Father while rejecting the Son, because the Son is how the Father is made known. Whoever openly confesses the Son has the Father as well.
Hold on to the gospel you heard at the start. Its value is not simply that it is old; it is the true message about Christ. If it stays in you, you will stay joined to the Son and the Father.
What Christ has promised is eternal life. Only God can give a gift that great, and it belongs to those who stay in the truth about his Son.
John explains why he has written all this: to warn them about people trying to lead them astray. A good shepherd both feeds the flock and guards it from wolves.

The Spirit they received from Christ stays with them and teaches them the truth. Saying they "do not need anyone to teach" them does not do away with pastors and teachers. It means they do not need the false teachers' new ideas, because the Spirit already confirms the truth they have. So they should remain in Christ.
With warm affection, John urges them to stay in Christ. Then, when Jesus returns, they can meet him with calm confidence instead of shrinking back in shame.

Since God is righteous, everyone who keeps doing what is right has been born of him, like children who resemble their father. Doing right does not earn this new birth. It shows the new birth has already happened.
